translations.text: A sermon by our holy father John Chrysostom for New Sunday.
And on the unbelief of the apostle Thomas. I come to repay you a debt.
A debt that benefits me who pay it and enriches you as well. I have come again to speak about Thomas,
who at first did not believe in the Lord’s resurrection, but afterward, through seeing and touching,
believed and acknowledged him as Christ and God. Open your minds wide, therefore, I beg you,
and receive my humble words with gentleness, so that you may gain some small benefit from them.
When the Savior had suddenly torn open the whole belly of Hades,
and had become the firstborn among the dead, and had entered through closed doors to his disciples,
Thomas, called the Twin, was not with them. The one longed for came, but the one who longed for him was absent. The good shepherd approached the flock,
but the sheep was wandering outside the fold. The king came, but the soldier was marching far away. For it was
a mystery of God’s providence that the disciple did not come.
For if he had come, he would not have disputed; if he had not disputed, he would not have examined; if he had not examined, he would not have believed in this way.
If he had not believed, he would not have taught us to believe in this way. Thus the disciple’s unbelief became the mother of our faith.
For this reason, although we do not see Christ, we worship him, because Thomas saw him and worshiped him. For this reason, examining him,
we praise him without having examined him, because Thomas held the Master with his own hands and praised him.
When Thomas came afterward, the other disciples said to him, “We have seen the Lord.
We have seen him who said, ‘After three days I will rise,’ and we have found his words proved true by his deeds.
We have seen him who said, ‘I am the resurrection and the life and the truth,’ and resurrection and life and truth
we have received from Life. We have seen him who said, ‘I have authority to lay down my life,
and I have authority to take it up again,’ and we have experienced his power through his deeds.
For the Savior suddenly entered the room without opening the doors.
Astonished at his marvelous arrival, we wondered at the new way in which he had entered.
We saw his hands, with which he crushed death, and in which he received the sharp points of the nails
and wiped away human sins. We also saw his holy side, wounded for our sake,
which poured out blood and water, the two drops of our salvation.” Thomas thought and said to them, “You have seen God [?]
You have seen him. Am I alone unworthy to see him? Was I not called just as you were called?
Was I not honored by him just as you were honored? Did I not also see him crucified, just as you did?
Just as I saw the sorrowful things with you, I also want to see the joyful things.
Just as I saw Christ’s death, I also want to see his resurrection.
For unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands and put my finger into the marks of the nails,
and put my hands into his side, I will not believe.
Persist, Thomas, in your excellent unbelief. Strive earnestly until you take hold of the anchor of faith.
Persist wholeheartedly in such longing until you see the one you long for, just as you desire. I love the divided mind of your thoughts.
For, rejecting every divided mind, I praise your contentious and Christ-loving understanding,
while rejecting all contentiousness. Disbelieve, disbelieve,
and do so still more, so that I too may believe with certainty. Seek God and call upon him who has come,
so that, while you seek him and call upon him, I too may embrace my deliverer.
Unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands, I will not believe.
Let me see with my own eyes what you have reported. For [?] the eyes are more trustworthy than hearing.
Then I will accept your account as well. I will put my finger into the wounds made by the nails,
and then I will believe the miracle. With this hand of mine I will thoroughly examine
the side that was pierced for my sake. Then I will bow before him who has returned to us from death, for I take pleasure in tangible things.
For I cannot rely on words alone.
While Thomas was saying these things to the apostles, Jesus came in among them, although the doors were shut.
The door of life entered through closed doors. He entered in a way that he alone knows.
For just as he was born without breaking the doors of virginity, so he was found inside the house without opening the lock.
And just as he came out of the tomb while the tomb was shut, so he entered in the flesh
where he already was in his divinity, without opening the doors. For he entered, forbidding [?],
and no one wished everything to come together [?]. He wished creation to serve.
His birth surpassed all words, and his departure from the tomb surpasses every thought.
And his entrance among the disciples is beyond words and beyond explanation.
For I have learned that he entered among the disciples, but how he entered I have not learned at all.
And what I have not received, I do not dare to speak of. I praise him who entered,
but I do not probe too deeply into the manner of his entrance. I proclaim the mystery,
but I do not explain what cannot be explained. I marvel at the sign that occurred, but I do not investigate how it happened.
I believe what is written and am saved, for I am obedient to the Master's miracles,
and not an investigator of God's works. But if someone among the Jews says, “You speak of impossible and strange things,
and [?] things unseen in nature. For how can flesh pass through closed doors?” I will say to him:
“How could the angel bring Habakkuk down into the lions' den and bring him back up again,
while leaving the seals upon it intact? A servant did what he wished,
but could the Master not do what he undertook?” Just as that happened when God willed it,
so too this was accomplished by the Son of God who had become man. Thus he entered among his disciples,
as the Savior willed, and stood in their midst so that he might appear to them all alike. And he said to them, “Peace be with you.
I bestow peace upon you. What I am, that I give you. This peace will subject all your enemies
beneath your feet. This peace will establish victory throughout the world.” And the disciples rejoiced again.
They delighted in the Master's appearance and voice, and nudged Thomas with their elbows and signaled with their eyes.
They all but spoke to him with their eyebrows: “Did we not tell you before, ‘We have seen the Lord,’ and you did not believe our words?
Look, the one you longed for stands before you himself. Delight in him as you asked; satisfy yourself as you thirsted.
Come to him who came to us for your salvation, and receive the resolution of what you sought.”
But Thomas stood directing his eyes over all the Savior's limbs,
examining each one and asking himself whether it was truly the same one who had suffered and risen who had come.
What, then, did the only good one, the only lover of mankind, say to him,
he who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth? “Bring your finger here and see my hands.
For your sake I have come to you; for your sake I have drawn near again, though in my divinity I had never withdrawn.
For your sake I offered these hands of mine to the nails, so that today I might lead you to safe pastures.
Draw near to me in body, spirit, and faith, and learn clearly what you have desired to learn.
Examine as you wish, and learn as you wish.
Read on my hand the writing of my voluntary suffering. Writing.
I submit all my judgments to you for examination. I am not ashamed of the wounds on my body.
I am not ashamed of the sores on my flesh, which I received because of your sores.
I do not hide my glory, the victory of my triumph; rather, it is manifest to all creation.
For the sun knows this too. That is why it withdrew, making night during the day.
The earth knows this too. That is why it sought a place of refuge. The dead know it too.
That is why they came out of their tombs. The curtain of the temple also learned of it.
That is why it tore apart and lamented the destruction of the Jews. You saw my hands as you wished.
You reached with your own finger into the wounds that do not close. Do you also wish to examine my side? I will bare that for you too.
Bring your [?] and inquisitive hand and put it into my side.
Touch my flesh, formed without human seed. Touch the flesh that suffered by my own will.
Touch my flesh, which was put to death for your sake, but was not swallowed up
by the corruption of death. Touch my flesh, which is [?] to the cherubim
and honored by the seraphim, and feared by the bodiless powers. And learn through this examination
what in me can be examined and what cannot, what in me is subject to suffering and what is beyond suffering,
what in me is mortal, what was put to death for your sake, and what remained untouched by death,
what it is that comes beneath your fingers, and what does not come beneath your right hand.
Do not be unbelieving, but believing. Do you seek to see the bones? Do you wish to see them?
Look, this is why I have left my side like this: so that you may search and examine it
and have faith and be saved; so that, when I come to judge the living and the dead,
I may show the wound to my enemies and condemn the assembly that fights against God,
so that the Jews may see the one whom they pierced and bow down, groaning.
Then Thomas answered and said, “My Lord and my God! I believe in your resurrection, Lord.”
I believe; I am overcome [?], O King. I believe; I no longer seek the one I have found.
I believe, Lord, and I no longer test [?], my Master, so severely, and I believe.
I will no longer burden your majesty with words. I know what I have held, and I do not dispute. I know whom I have been deemed worthy to touch.
I know the one whom not even death itself can hold for long. I know whom I must honor.
Therefore I say, “My Lord and my God.” You are my God and Lord, both before all ages and new.
You are heavenly and earthly. You are invisible and visible. You are unknown and became known for my sake.
You are without form, yet in this form. You are truly God and truly human. You are in heaven.
You are on the cross. You are on the royal throne. You are on the nails and on the wood.
You are free from suffering in spirit. You suffer in the flesh. You are free from death, being of one substance with the Father.
You are in death. You are in life. You are among the dead; you are above death. You were dead for three days.
You exist forever with your Father. You raised up the temple of flesh. You rose by your own power.
You are with us in the flesh, and wholly present throughout all creation. You fill all things. You were held by me.
I see you with eyes of flesh. I perceive you with eyes of faith.
I have recognized your Father’s divinity in you. I confess you alone as Lord and God. One thing, and another.
I have learned to know you as one. I have not known you as one and another. I do not divide you, who are undivided.
I do not separate you, who are inseparable. I do not cut you apart, who are undivided. What I see and what I hold,
and what I perceive, I have confessed with one voice: “My Lord and my God.”
By your descent you raised my soul from the unfathomable depths.
You had mercy on people who had been captives. You trampled the devil as much as you wished.
You condemned sin in the flesh. You put death to death in the flesh.
By incorruptibility you drove away corruption. By your resurrection,
you renewed resurrection for us. You left the three-day tomb on earth as a pledge to the dead
of resurrection. You showed people to be heavenly. The earth, brighter than heaven,
you made. You changed everything for the better. You, being God, became human, so that you might make the human being God.
“My God, my God.” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me?”
Take care that, when I ascend again in the flesh, you do not take up words of unbelief and say:
“Unless I see the mark of the nail in his hands, I will not believe.”
Once he longed; once he disbelieved; once he examined.
Once he believed. What he received has already been proclaimed. For blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.
For that blessing will pass to us, to those who have not seen him and have believed in him.
For blessed are we who have seen the invisible one through faith. Blessed are we who celebrate the feast and behold him,
bringing him to our eyes, kissing him with our lips, and eating him with our teeth.
O wondrous and exalted mystery! He who sits at the right hand of the Father
is found at the right hand of the devout, and he who is praised by angels is held by defiled hands.
Offered by the unworthy, he offers himself, and he does not flee from our sinful palm.
He does not flee from our condemned fingers, nor does the Creator destroy those made of clay.
But he himself commanded and says, “Take, eat. Take, drink. Bring your hands
and put them into my side, and take delight in my vessels. For whichever vessel you take,
I am wholly in it.” Let us all, then, come in purity to the pure one, and let us receive our Lord.
After receiving him there, let us not immediately [?], nor approach him with contempt, but let us withdraw into ourselves.
And let us each speak alone to our Savior, saying to the Lord:
“We are not worthy for you to come beneath the roof of our souls. But since you wish to be held by us,
in your love for humanity, be pleased also to dwell in us to the end. Trusting in you, we approach.
You command us, Master, to lift up the gates of our mouths, which you alone have made.
You enter in your love for humanity, as before. You enter and loosen the bonds of lawlessness.
You enter and illuminate our dark thoughts. We believe that you will do this.
For [?] the prostitute who fled to you with tears did not go away [?].
Nor did you leave the robber as he was, nor reject the tax collector who repented, nor drive away the persecutor who acknowledged your kingdom.
But all of them were received by you through repentance, and you enrolled them among your friends.”
So, with such a prayer and such a disposition of soul, let us receive the heavenly mysteries.
And let us protect ourselves by chaste living. Let no filthy word come out where Christ enters.
You too, newly enlightened, must lead such a life. Honor your painless birth; do not reject the holy baptismal font.
Let the font not say of you, “I bore children and raised them, but they rejected me.”
Your names are written in heaven. Do not soil yourselves again in the mire of pleasure through evil deeds.
When you take off your white robes, do not take off the whiteness of your souls. For if
you yourselves do not cast off that garment, no one else will be able to strip it from you. Always remain newly enlightened,
so that you may be worthy of that blessed call: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father.
Receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the whole world.”
May none of us fail to attain it, in Christ Jesus our Lord,
to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
